title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E510 treats the critical height at which a vertical column buckles under its own weight. In modern terms this is the heavy-column problem EI y''' + q x y' = 0. It reduces to an Airy-type equation u'' + (q/EI) x u = 0 for the slope, whose solutions are Bessel functions J_{±1/3}. On the previous page Euler reduced the problem to finding the number t that satisfies the transcendental equation P + PQ' − QP' = 0. P, P', Q and Q' are four alternating power series in t. Once t is found, the height b is scaled to a test column of known strength through the earlier Euler load Γ = π²Ekk/a².

This page (§32) is purely a computational scheme. Each series is written as a sum of terms I, II, III, … The successive terms of P are generated recursively in common logarithms: log(term n+1) = log(term n) + log t − log c_n.

Checking the constants shows c_n = (3n−1)(3n)(3n+1)/(3n−2): 24, 52.5, 102.857, 171.6, 258.46, … So, up to the sign alternation that is handled separately, the series is
P = 1 − t/(2·3·4) + 1·4·t²/(2·3···7) − 1·4·7·t³/(2···10) + … = Σ (−t)^n · 1·4···(3n−2)/(3n+1)!.

This is the even Airy-type series Σ (−t)^n · 1·4···(3n−2)/(3n)! integrated once. The right column gives the companion series P' term by term as (term of P)/(3n+2), with divisors 5, 8, 11, …, 59. That amounts to one further integration. The first term I' is not listed; presumably it is 1/2.

On the next page (§33) Q has ratio constants (n+1)(3n+1)(3n+2)/n: 6, 40, 84, 146.67, … So Q = Σ (−1)^{n−1} 3^{n−1}(n−1)! t^n/(3n)!, and Q' = Q term/(3n+1).

The point of the tabulation: Euler can compute 20 terms of each series for several trial values of t (§34 begins with the bound t < 266 from the previous memoir). He then interpolates the root, i.e. regula falsi by repeated trial. Computing in logarithms avoids the large factorials.
errors: All 19 logarithmic constants on this page check against log[(3n−1)(3n)(3n+1)/(3n−2)] to 7 decimals (e.g. log 24 = 1.3802112, log 52.5 = 1.7201593, log(720/7) = 2.0122340, log(1716/10) = 2.2345173, …, log(185136/55) = 3.5271282). No numerical errors were found on this page.

Outside this page, on the next page (§33): the constant for l XIII in the Q table reads 3.1727474. With n = 12 the correct value is log(13·37·38/12) = log 1523.17 = 3.1827474, so either the print or the transcription has slipped a digit. If the error is in the print, it would affect Euler's numerical evaluation of Q for large t.

Outside this page, on the previous page: the transcribed final formula b = a·∛(λbb/(ππdd)) is dimensionally inconsistent. From the definitions it should presumably read b = a·∛(λt/ππ) or similar. This should be checked against the image of p.183.
Physical correctness of the whole approach (boundary conditions in the heavy-column problem) is a known historical issue for Euler's 1778 column papers. It is not decidable from this page alone.

ideas.what: Recursive logarithmic generation of terms of alternating power series (term ratios precomputed as log constants) for repeated evaluation at trial values of a parameter
ideas.modern_name: Term-ratio recurrence / hypergeometric term evaluation; numerical root finding by trial and interpolation

ideas.what: Series P = Σ(−t)^n·1·4···(3n−2)/(3n+1)! and its further integral P', i.e. integrated Airy-type series arising from the heavy column
ideas.modern_name: Integrals of Airy functions / Bessel functions J_{±1/3} (hypergeometric 1F2-type series)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Heavy-column solution: Greenhill 1881. Airy function: Airy 1838. Series solutions of y'' + xy = 0 were known to Euler earlier.
ideas.where_published: E510 itself, and related column memoirs of 1778 (Acta Acad. Petrop. 1778); discussed in Todhunter–Pearson's History of Elasticity

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a correct but routine table of logarithmic term-ratio constants for evaluating the series. The underlying heavy-column problem and Euler's 1778 attempts are well known in histories of elasticity, with Greenhill credited for the definitive solution. Nothing here appears new.
transcription_corrections: Transcription of this page matches the image. The printed fraction 1/23 for VIII' and 1/26 for IX' are consistent with the 1/(3n+2) pattern.
The next page's 'l XIII … − 3,1727474' should be checked against the print. Mathematically it should be 3,1827474.
